questions.question: A retailer rents extra computing capacity for its two-week holiday sale and stops paying for it when the sale ends. Which model does this describe?
questions.explanation: In the consumption-based model you pay only for the resources you use, when you use them. There is no upfront hardware purchase and no paying for idle capacity once the peak has passed.

questions.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which item is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility, whatever the cloud service type?
questions.explanation: The provider always owns the physical datacenter, network and hosts. The customer always owns their data, the devices that connect, and the accounts and identities that can reach their cloud resources.

questions.question: A hospital must keep patient records in its own datacenter but wants to use public cloud capacity for seasonal demand spikes. Which cloud model fits best?
questions.explanation: A hybrid cloud combines a private environment with a public cloud. Sensitive workloads stay in the private environment while the public cloud absorbs temporary demand.

questions.question: Which is a typical drawback of a private cloud compared with a public cloud?
options: Your data shares hardware with other tenants
You have less control over security
You cannot run it in your own datacenter
Higher cost, because you buy and maintain the hardware
questions.explanation: A private cloud gives you full control, but your organisation pays for and maintains the hardware, so it usually costs more and scales less quickly than a public cloud.

questions.question: Which statement best describes serverless computing?
options: There are no physical servers involved anywhere
You write the code, and the platform provisions, scales and runs the infrastructure, charging for actual usage
You manage the operating system but not the application
It can only run inside an on-premises datacenter
questions.explanation: Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you do not manage them. The platform handles provisioning and scaling, and you are typically billed for execution time or requests.

questions.question: A start-up wants to launch a product quickly without buying any hardware upfront. Which option is the best fit?
options: Waiting for a hardware refresh cycle
questions.explanation: Public cloud removes the upfront capital cost. You can provision resources in minutes and pay for them as an operating expense.

questions.question: Which statement describes high availability in the cloud?
options: The ability to resize a virtual machine
The ability to estimate monthly costs in advance
Keeping services running with minimal downtime, often backed by a service level agreement (SLA)
The ability to move workloads to another cloud provider
questions.explanation: High availability is about keeping workloads accessible. Providers express it as an SLA, such as a percentage of uptime they commit to.

questions.question: Traffic to a web app suddenly increases tenfold, and you add more identical instances to share the load. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling adds more instances of a resource. Vertical scaling instead makes one instance more powerful.

questions.question: Which action is an example of vertical scaling?
options: Adding five more virtual machines behind a load balancer
Increasing the CPU and memory of an existing virtual machine
Deploying the app to a second region
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up or down) changes the capability of a single resource, for example moving a VM to a larger size.

questions.question: A system can recover from failures and keep functioning. Which cloud benefit does this describe?
questions.explanation: Reliability is the ability of a system to recover from failures and continue to work. It is a pillar of the Azure Well-Architected Framework.

questions.question: Which cloud benefit lets you use templates so that every deployed resource meets your organisation's standards?
questions.explanation: Governance in the cloud uses templates, policies and auditing so that deployments meet technical and regulatory standards, and non-compliant resources can be flagged.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of management OF the cloud (as opposed to management IN the cloud)?
options: Creating a VM with the Azure CLI
Browsing resources in the web portal
Automatically scaling resources up and down based on demand
questions.explanation: Management of the cloud covers what the cloud does for you, such as autoscaling, template deployment and automatic health monitoring. Management in the cloud is the tooling you use: portal, CLI, APIs and PowerShell.

questions.question: A team is migrating a legacy application that needs a specific operating system configuration. Which service type gives them the control they need?
options: None, the cloud cannot host legacy apps
questions.explanation: IaaS gives you virtual machines and networking that you configure yourself, including the operating system. That control suits lift-and-shift migrations of existing applications.

questions.question: Developers want to deploy a web API without patching servers or managing the operating system. Which service type fits?
questions.explanation: PaaS provides a managed environment for building and deploying applications. The provider runs the operating system, runtime and underlying infrastructure.

questions.question: Employees use a hosted email and calendar service that the provider manages entirely. Which service type is this?
questions.explanation: SaaS delivers a finished application. The provider manages everything from infrastructure to the app, and you manage your data, users and settings.

questions.question: In which service type does the customer take on the MOST management responsibility?
questions.explanation: With IaaS you manage the operating system, patches, middleware, apps and data. Responsibility shifts toward the provider as you move to PaaS and then SaaS.

questions.question: Which statement about PaaS is correct?
options: The customer manages the physical hardware
The provider manages the OS and runtime, and the customer manages application code and data
The customer receives a complete finished application
The customer must install operating system patches
questions.explanation: In PaaS the provider takes care of the infrastructure, operating systems and runtimes. You focus on your code and data.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of an IaaS offering?
questions.explanation: Azure Virtual Machines lets you rent virtual servers and manage the OS yourself, which is IaaS. App Service and Functions are PaaS or serverless, and Microsoft 365 is SaaS.

questions.question: What is an Azure region?
options: A geographic area containing one or more datacenters connected by a low-latency network
questions.explanation: A region is a set of datacenters deployed within a latency-defined perimeter and connected through a dedicated regional low-latency network. You choose a region when you deploy most resources.

questions.question: Which statement best describes availability zones?
options: Groups of regions in the same country
Physically separate locations within a region, each with independent power, cooling and networking
questions.explanation: Availability zones protect against datacenter-level failures. Each zone is a separate physical location within a region, so a problem in one zone does not take down the others.

questions.question: Why does Azure pair regions within a geography?
options: Every Azure service replicates all data between the pair automatically
To support disaster recovery: recovery of one region in each pair is prioritised in a wide outage, and planned updates are rolled out one region at a time
To double the price of resources
So that subscriptions can only be used in two regions
questions.explanation: Region pairs help with resilience. Azure prioritises restoring one region of each pair during a broad outage and applies platform updates sequentially. Replication of your data still depends on the service and the options you choose.

questions.question: Which is the correct hierarchy, from highest level to lowest?
options: Subscription, management group, resource group, resource
Resource group, subscription, management group, resource
Management group, subscription, resource group, resource
Resource, resource group, subscription, management group
questions.explanation: Management groups contain subscriptions, subscriptions contain resource groups, and resource groups contain resources. Policies and access assigned higher up are inherited downward.

questions.question: Which statement about Azure resource groups is true?
options: A resource can belong to several resource groups at the same time
Resource groups can be nested inside one another
A resource belongs to exactly one resource group at a time
Deleting a resource group leaves its resources untouched
questions.explanation: Each resource lives in exactly one resource group. Resource groups cannot be nested, and deleting one deletes every resource inside it.

questions.question: You need to apply the same Azure Policy to ten different subscriptions in one action. Which container should you use?
questions.explanation: Management groups sit above subscriptions. Assigning a policy or access rule to a management group applies it to every subscription beneath it.

questions.question: Which Azure compute option runs your code in response to events, bills per execution and needs no server management?
questions.explanation: Azure Functions is event-driven serverless compute. You supply the code, and Azure runs and scales it, billing for what executes.

questions.question: Which resource lets you automatically add or remove identical VMs as load changes?
questions.explanation: Virtual Machine Scale Sets manage a group of load-balanced, identical VMs and can scale the number of instances up or down automatically.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an availability set?
options: To spread VMs across fault domains and update domains so one hardware failure or maintenance event does not take them all down
questions.explanation: An availability set arranges VMs across separate fault domains (hardware) and update domains (maintenance), reducing the impact of a single failure or planned update.

questions.question: Which service gives a private, dedicated connection from an on-premises network to Azure that does NOT travel over the public internet?
questions.explanation: ExpressRoute uses a private connection through a connectivity provider. A VPN Gateway also connects on-premises networks but sends encrypted traffic over the public internet.

questions.question: What does virtual network (VNet) peering do?
options: Encrypts data stored in a VNet
Connects two virtual networks so resources can communicate privately over the Microsoft backbone network
Translates domain names to IP addresses
Creates a backup of a VNet
questions.explanation: Peering links virtual networks so their resources talk using private IP addresses, with traffic staying on the Microsoft backbone rather than the public internet.

questions.question: What is a private endpoint?
options: A public IP address for a virtual machine
A network interface in your virtual network with a private IP address that connects you privately to an Azure service
A firewall rule that blocks all traffic
questions.explanation: A private endpoint brings an Azure service, such as a storage account, into your virtual network with a private IP address, so traffic does not need to use the public endpoint.

questions.question: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
options: Containers each include a full guest operating system
Containers share the host operating system kernel, so they are lighter and start faster
Containers always require a physical server
questions.explanation: Containers package an app and its dependencies but share the host OS kernel. This makes them smaller and faster to start than VMs, which each carry a full guest operating system.

questions.question: Which Azure Storage service provides fully managed file shares that can be accessed over SMB?
questions.explanation: Azure Files offers managed file shares in the cloud that you can mount from Windows, Linux and macOS using the SMB protocol (and NFS for some tiers).

questions.question: Which storage service is best for large amounts of unstructured data such as images, video and backups?
questions.explanation: Blob Storage is optimised for massive amounts of unstructured data such as images, documents, video and backup files.

questions.question: Which access tier has the lowest storage cost for data that is rarely accessed and can tolerate hours of retrieval delay?
questions.explanation: The Archive tier is the cheapest to store but the data is offline. It must be rehydrated before use, which can take hours. Hot suits frequent access, with Cool and Cold in between.

questions.question: Which redundancy option copies your data synchronously across three availability zones in the primary region?
questions.explanation: ZRS replicates data across three availability zones in one region, protecting against a datacenter failure. LRS keeps three copies inside a single datacenter.

questions.question: Which option helps protect your data from a complete regional outage?
questions.explanation: GRS also copies data to a secondary region far from the primary, so the data survives the loss of the whole primary region. LRS and ZRS keep data in one region.

questions.question: Which command-line tool is optimised for copying data to and from Azure storage accounts?
questions.explanation: AzCopy is a command-line utility for fast, scriptable transfers to and from Blob and File storage. Storage Explorer is the graphical equivalent.

questions.question: A company has hundreds of terabytes to move to Azure but only a slow internet link. Which option is best?
options: Azure Data Box (a physical transfer device)
questions.explanation: Azure Data Box is a physical appliance you fill with data and ship to Microsoft, which uploads it for you. It is designed for very large transfers where network speed is a bottleneck.

questions.question: Which service keeps an on-premises Windows file server in sync with Azure Files?
questions.explanation: Azure File Sync turns a Windows Server into a cache of an Azure file share, keeping local and cloud copies in sync. Azure Migrate is for assessing and moving servers and workloads.

questions.question: Which Azure service provides cloud-based identity and access management for users and apps?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is Microsoft's cloud identity and access management service.

questions.question: Which sign-in is an example of multifactor authentication?
options: A password followed by a second password
A password followed by approving a prompt on your phone
A very long passphrase on its own
questions.explanation: MFA combines factors from different categories: something you know (password), something you have (phone) and something you are (biometric). Two passwords are still one category.

questions.question: A support engineer must be able to restart virtual machines in one resource group but do nothing else. What should you use?
options: Azure role-based access control (RBAC) with a role assigned at that resource group
questions.explanation: RBAC grants permissions by assigning roles at a scope. Scoping the role to one resource group follows the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: You want users to be asked for MFA only when they sign in from outside the corporate network. Which feature do you use?
questions.explanation: Conditional Access applies if-then rules to sign-ins. Signals such as location, device or risk decide whether to allow, block or require extra verification like MFA.

questions.question: Which set of principles describes Zero Trust?
options: Trust everything inside the corporate network by default
Verify explicitly, use least-privilege access and assume breach
Rely on a single strong perimeter firewall
questions.explanation: Zero Trust treats every request as untrusted until verified. It verifies explicitly, limits access to what is needed, and assumes an attacker may already be inside.

questions.question: What does the defense-in-depth model describe?
options: Relying on one very strong security control
Using multiple layers of protection, such as physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application and data
Keeping all data in one datacenter
questions.explanation: Defense in depth layers several protections so that if one layer is breached, the others still slow or stop an attacker.

questions.question: Which service provides security posture management and threat protection for workloads in Azure and hybrid environments?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender for Cloud assesses your security posture, recommends improvements and provides threat protection across Azure, hybrid and multicloud workloads.

questions.question: What does single sign-on (SSO) let a user do?
options: Use the same password for every website
Sign in once and access multiple applications without entering credentials again
questions.explanation: With SSO a user authenticates once with their identity provider and then gets access to multiple apps, reducing password fatigue while keeping central control.

questions.question: Which factor can change the price of the same virtual machine size?
options: The region where it is deployed
The name of its resource group
The display name of the subscription
questions.explanation: Costs vary by region because of local factors such as infrastructure and energy costs. Resource type, size, usage and bandwidth also affect cost, but names and tags do not.

questions.question: Which tool estimates the cost of Azure resources you are planning to deploy?
questions.explanation: The Pricing Calculator lets you configure services and see an estimate before you deploy. It estimates planned spend, whereas Cost Management analyses what you actually spend.

questions.question: Which capability lets you analyse your actual spending, set budgets and receive cost alerts?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Cost Management provides cost analysis, budgets and alerts for your actual Azure usage.

questions.question: You want to see how much each department spends on Azure. What helps most?
options: Applying a tag such as department to resources and grouping costs by that tag
questions.explanation: Tags are name-value pairs you attach to resources. In cost analysis you can group or filter by tag to attribute spend to teams, projects or environments.

questions.question: Which option lowers the price of steady, predictable workloads when you commit to one or three years of use?
questions.explanation: Azure reservations give a discount compared with pay-as-you-go prices in exchange for a one-year or three-year commitment, which suits stable workloads.

questions.question: A dev VM is not needed overnight. What stops the compute charges while keeping its disks?
options: Shutting down the operating system from inside the VM
questions.explanation: If you only shut down the OS, the VM stays allocated and still incurs compute charges. Stopping it (deallocating) through Azure releases the compute, though you still pay for the disks.

questions.question: Which service lets you create rules, for example allowing resources to be deployed only in approved regions?
questions.explanation: Azure Policy defines and enforces standards for resources, and evaluates how compliant your existing resources are.

questions.question: How can you stop even subscription owners from accidentally deleting a critical resource?
questions.explanation: Resource locks override user permissions. A CanNotDelete lock lets authorised users read and modify a resource but prevents deletion until the lock is removed.

questions.question: Which service helps you discover, classify and govern data across on-premises, multicloud and SaaS sources?
questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview is a data governance and compliance service for mapping, classifying and managing data across your whole estate.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Azure Policy and Azure RBAC?
options: They do exactly the same thing
Policy controls what resource configurations are allowed, and RBAC controls what actions users are allowed to take
RBAC controls pricing and Policy controls networking
questions.explanation: RBAC answers who can do what. Policy answers what resources may look like, regardless of who is deploying them. Use them together.

questions.question: What does a ReadOnly lock on a resource do?
options: Authorised users can read the resource but cannot modify or delete it
It hides the resource from everyone
It only blocks deletion but allows changes
questions.explanation: A ReadOnly lock is like giving everyone the Reader role on that resource: it can be viewed but not changed or deleted. CanNotDelete allows changes but blocks deletion.

questions.question: You apply a CanNotDelete lock to a resource group. What happens to the resources inside it?
options: Nothing, the lock applies to the group only
They inherit the lock, so they cannot be deleted either
They are moved to a new subscription
questions.explanation: Locks are inherited by child resources. A lock on a resource group or subscription also protects everything inside it.

questions.question: Which tool is a web-based console for creating and managing Azure resources?
questions.explanation: The Azure portal is the browser-based graphical interface for managing resources, dashboards and subscriptions.

questions.question: Which tool gives you a browser-accessible shell, with Bash or PowerShell, and needs no local installation?
questions.explanation: Azure Cloud Shell is an authenticated shell you open from the browser. It comes with the Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell already available.

questions.question: Which statement about Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell is correct?
options: They are both command-line tools that can automate Azure tasks, using az commands and cmdlets such as New-AzVM respectively
Only Azure CLI can create virtual machines
They only work from the portal
Azure PowerShell can only run on Windows Server
questions.explanation: Both can create and manage resources and be scripted. Azure CLI uses az commands. Azure PowerShell uses cmdlets such as New-AzVM. Both run on Windows, macOS and Linux.

questions.question: Which service extends Azure management to servers and Kubernetes clusters running outside Azure, such as on-premises or in other clouds?
questions.explanation: Azure Arc projects non-Azure resources into Azure so you can manage and govern them with the same tools, policies and RBAC.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of infrastructure as code (IaC)?
options: Repeatable, consistent deployments defined in code that can be version-controlled
It removes the need for any security
It only works for on-premises servers
questions.explanation: IaC describes infrastructure in files, so deployments are repeatable, reviewable, testable and consistent. It reduces manual configuration errors.

questions.question: Which statement describes Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
options: The deployment and management service that provides a consistent management layer for all Azure tools, including the portal and CLI
questions.explanation: Whether you use the portal, CLI, PowerShell or an API, your request goes through Azure Resource Manager, which authenticates it, applies RBAC and policy, and carries out the change.

questions.question: ARM templates are described as idempotent. What does that mean?
options: They can only be deployed once
Deploying the same template repeatedly produces the same resulting state
They only work in the portal
questions.explanation: ARM templates are declarative: they state the desired result, and redeploying them leaves your environment in that same state. Bicep is a simpler language that compiles to ARM templates.

questions.question: Which service gives personalised recommendations to improve reliability, security, performance, cost and operational excellence?
questions.explanation: Azure Advisor analyses your resources and suggests best-practice improvements across those categories.

questions.question: Where do you find notices about Azure service issues and planned maintenance that affect your resources?
questions.explanation: Azure Service Health gives a personalised view of Azure platform incidents, planned maintenance and advisories relevant to the services and regions you use.

questions.question: Which service collects, analyses and acts on telemetry from both cloud and on-premises environments?
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor gathers metrics and logs, lets you analyse them, and can raise alerts or trigger automated actions.

questions.question: Which Azure Monitor tool lets you query log data using the Kusto Query Language (KQL)?
questions.explanation: Log Analytics is the tool in the portal for writing and running KQL queries over data stored in Azure Monitor Logs.

questions.question: Which feature monitors the performance and availability of a web application and helps detect exceptions?
questions.explanation: Application Insights is the application performance monitoring feature of Azure Monitor. It tracks requests, failures, dependencies and user behaviour.

questions.question: You want an email whenever a VM's CPU stays above 90% for five minutes. Which feature do you use?
questions.explanation: Azure Monitor alerts evaluate metrics or logs against a condition and notify people or run actions when it is met.
